parole.testo: From Middle English arvell, from Old Norse erfiǫl (“a funeral feast”), from arfr (“inheritance”) + öl (“ale”). Cognate with Danish arveøl (“a wake, funeral feast”). More at erf, ale.

parole.significato: A kind of spear-like polearm used by the Norse, conventionally translated as halberd, but of uncertain precise nature.
parole.testo: From Old Norse atgeirr or Icelandic atgeir.

parole.significato: From side to side, often in an oblique manner; across or over.

parole.significato: An elf.
parole.testo: From Old Norse álfr.

parole.testo: From Middle English axil, in turn a combination of Old English eax and Old Norse ǫxull.

parole.significato: Always; ever; continually; for an indefinite time.

parole.significato: Ever, always.

parole.testo: From Middle English bain, bayne, bayn, beyn (“direct, prompt”), from Old Norse beinn (“straight, right, favourable, advantageous, convenient, friendly, fair, keen”).

parole.significato: Having the manners of a child; childish; silly.
parole.testo: From Middle English *bernis, *barnisch, from Old English *bearnisċ and Old Norse bernskr (“childish”), from Proto-Germanic *barniskaz (“childish”), equivalent to bairn + -ish. Cognate with Gothic 𐌱𐌰𐍂𐌽𐌹𐍃𐌺𐍃 (barnisks, “childish”).

parole.significato: To set dogs on (an animal etc.) to bite or worry; to attack with dogs, especially for sport.

parole.significato: A child.
parole.testo: From Middle English barn, bern, from Old English bearn (“child, son, offspring, progeny”) and Old Norse barn (“child”). Doublet of bairn. Cognate to West Frisian bern (“child, children”), Middle Dutch baren (“child”).

parole.significato: To strike heavily; to beat.
parole.testo: From Middle English *basshen, *basken, likely from Old Norse *baska (“to strike”), akin to Swedish basa (“to baste, whip, lash, flog”), Danish baske (“to beat, strike, cudgel”), German patschen (“to slap”)

parole.significato: To bathe in warmth; to be exposed to pleasant heat.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English basken, from Old Norse baðask (“to take a bath”, literally “to bathe oneself”), mediopassive form from underlying baða (“to bathe”) + sik (“oneself”), from Proto-Germanic *baþōną and *sek. Doublet of English bathe.

parole.significato: To bellow, roar, or shout.

parole.significato: One or more kinds of barley, especially six-rowed barley.
parole.testo: From Middle English byge, from Old Norse bygg (“barley, probably Hordeum vulgare, common barley”), from Proto-Germanic *bewwuz (“crop, barley”). Cognate with Old English bēow (“barley”).

parole.testo: Perhaps from Middle English blot, blout (“soft; flexible; pliable”), from Old Norse blautr (“soft”). Akin to Danish blød, Dutch bloot (“nude”) and German bloß (“nude”).

parole.significato: A blossom; the flower of a plant; an expanded bud.
parole.testo: From Middle English blome, from Old Norse blóm, from Proto-Germanic *blōmô (“flower”). Doublet of bloom (“spongy mass of metal”); see there for more.

parole.significato: The trunk or stem of a tree.

parole.testo: From Middle English boon (“prayer”), from Old Norse bón (“prayer, petition”), from Proto-Germanic *bōniz (“supplication”), influenced by boon (“good, favorable”, adjective). Doublet of ben; see there for more.

parole.testo: From Old English burna, Old Norse brunnr. Doublet of bourn.

parole.significato: To tie, fasten.

parole.significato: A projecting piece left on a tree or shrub when a branch is severed; knob; stump.

parole.significato: Coat (something) with a crust of solid material.
parole.testo: From Middle English cake, from Old Norse kaka (“cake”) (compare Norwegian kake, Icelandic/Swedish kaka, Danish kage), from Proto-Germanic *kakǭ, of disputed origin. Likely a distant cognate with kaak. Perhaps related to cookie, kuchen, and quiche. Doublet of coca (pastry).

parole.significato: The back of the leg below the knee.
parole.testo: From Middle English calf, kalf, from Old Norse kalfi, possibly derived from the same Germanic root as English calf (“young cow”) (above). Cognate with Icelandic kálfi (“calf of the leg”).

parole.significato: A horse.
parole.testo: From Old Norse kapall, from Latin caballus. Doublet of cheval.

parole.significato: A rude, rustic man; a churl.
parole.testo: From Middle English carl, from Old English carl, a borrowing from Old Norse karl (“man, husband”), from Proto-Germanic *karilaz. Doublet of ceorl, churl, and karl.

parole.significato: A woman; also, a hag or witch.
parole.testo: From Old Norse karling, feminine of karl (“carl”).

parole.significato: Any marsh; marshy ground, swampland.
parole.testo: From Middle English kerr and Middle English carr meaning meadow, field or grassland of a low lying variety; possibly related to Old Norse kjarr. Compare Swedish kärr, Icelandic kjarr.

parole.significato: A small, open, wheeled vehicle, drawn or pushed by a person or animal, often with two wheels on one axle, more often us…

parole.significato: A gag.
parole.testo: From Middle English *kavel, kevel, from Old English cæfl (“gag, bit, muzzle”), possibly from or akin to Old Norse kafli, kefli (“a piece of wood, gag”).

parole.significato: The stick or runestaff used in casting lots; a lot.
parole.testo: From Middle English cavel, kavell, kevell, from Old Norse kafl, kafli (“long, round piece of wood, staff”), from Proto-Germanic *kablô, *kablaz. Compare also Middle Dutch kāvelen (“to draw lots, a lot”), kavele (“fate, lottery”), modern Dutch kavel (“lot, plot of land”), dialectal German Kabel.

parole.significato: The jaw.
parole.testo: Inherited from Northern Middle English chaft, from Old Norse kjaptr, kjǫptr.

parole.testo: From Middle English childbyrth [and other forms], perhaps a partial calque of Old Norse barnburðr (“childbearing, childbirth”, literally “bairn birth”); equivalent to child + birth. Compare Swedish barnsbörd (“childbirth”), Icelandic barnsburður (“childbirth”).

parole.significato: a blood-sucking fly of the family Tabanidae: gadfly, horsefly, deer fly, blind-fly, tabanid
parole.testo: From Middle English clege, from Old Norse kleggi. Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk klegg. Possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *glōgʰ-s (“point”); compare Ancient Greek γλωχίς (glōkhís, “barb”).

parole.significato: To cut, especially with scissors or shears as opposed to a knife etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English clippen, from Old Norse klippa (“to clip, cut the hair, shear sheep”). Cognate with Icelandic klippa (“to clip”), Swedish klippa (“to clip”), Danish klippe (“to clip”), Norwegian Bokmål klippe (“to clip”).

parole.significato: To split; separate; cleave; chop.
parole.testo: From Middle English cliven, from Old Norse klyfja, klufða (“to split, chop, cleave”), from Proto-Germanic *kleubaną (“to split, pick”), from Proto-Indo-European *glewbʰ- (“to cut, carve, peel”). Cognate with Old English clēofan (“to cleave, split, separate”). Doublet of cleave.

parole.significato: A heavy object, often a kind of stick, intended for use as a bludgeoning weapon or a plaything.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English clubbe, from Old Norse klubba, klumba (“cudgel”), from Proto-Germanic *klumpô (“clip, clasp; clump, lump; log, block”). Cognate with English clump, cloud, Latin globus, glomus; and perhaps related to Middle Low German kolve (“bulb”), German Kolben (“butt, bulb, club”).

parole.significato: To numb; benumb; stiffen or paralyse with cold or fear

parole.significato: A brood of chickens or a sitting of bird, monotreme or reptile eggs; a sitting.
parole.testo: Variant form of cletch, from Middle English cleken (“to hatch”), perhaps from Old Norse klekja (“to hatch”).

parole.significato: A tooth on a gear.

parole.significato: A soft, moist, mild American cheese similar to cheddar, made with a washed-curd process.
parole.testo: From either the Old Norse personal name Koli or kol (“charcoal”) + býr (“settlement”).

parole.significato: In a cold or uncaring manner; indifferently.
parole.testo: From Middle English coldliche, caldeliche, perhaps borrowed from Old Norse kaldliga (“coldly”); equivalent to cold + -ly. Displaced Middle English colde (“coldly”), from Old English cealde (“coldly”).

parole.significato: Manner; way; means; available course; contrivance.

parole.significato: To exchange, barter.
parole.testo: From Middle English coupen (“to buy; (figuratively) to pay for”), from Old Norse kaupa (“to buy, bargain, barter, exchange”).

parole.significato: To intimidate; to daunt the spirits or courage of.
parole.testo: Probably from Old Norse kúga (“to oppress”) (whence also Norwegian and Danish kue, Swedish kuva); compare Icelandic kúfa (“to set on top”) and Faroese kúga (“to oppress”).

parole.significato: Any of several birds of the family Rallidae that have short bills.

parole.testo: From Middle English Dane, from Old Norse danir or Old English Dene. Both forms ultimately descend from Proto-Germanic *daniz.

parole.significato: A member of the race of Dǫkkálfar or Dark Alfs, creatures who live underground.
parole.testo: Back-formation from dark elves, a calque of Old Norse dǫkkalfar.

parole.significato: A malicious coward; a dishonorable sneak.
parole.testo: From Middle English dastard (“a dullard”), most likely formed from *dast, a base derived from Old Norse dæstr (“exhausted, breathless”) + -ard. parole.significato: To assuage; soften; mitigate; relieve; calm; alleviate (pain).
parole.testo: From Middle English deven, deaven (“to make deaf”), from Old English dēafian (“to wax or become deaf”) and Old Norse deyfa (“to make deaf, make blunt, numb, soothe, allay”). Cognate with dialectal Norwegian døyva (“to deafen, make dull”).

parole.significato: In a state of shock or confusion.

parole.significato: To stop living; to become dead; to undergo death.

parole.significato: Soil or earth.

parole.significato: To exhibit a conspicuous (sometimes malevolent) pleasure or sense of self-satisfaction, often at an adversary's misfort…
parole.testo: From Middle English *gloten, glouten, from Old Norse glotta (“to grin, smile scornfully”) or Old English *glotian, both from Proto-Germanic *glutōną (“to stare”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰel- (“to shine”), related to dialectal Swedish glotta, glutta (“to peep”), Middle High German glutzen, glotze

parole.significato: To gaze in alarm; be terrified; stare.
parole.testo: From Middle English glopen, probably from Old Norse glápa (“to stare vacantly”), from Proto-Germanic *glupaną (“to shine, gape”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰlub(ʰ)- (“to yawn, gape”). parole.significato: To be in fear; gaze in alarm or astonishment; look downcast
parole.testo: From Middle English glopnen, from Old Norse glúpna (“to frighten, grieve, look downcast”), from Proto-Germanic *glupnōną (“to frighten, cause to stare”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰlub(ʰ)- (“to yawn, gape”). Cognate with Icelandic glúpna (“to put to shame”). More at glope.

parole.significato: To gnaw; nibble; bite at (something)
parole.testo: From Middle English *gnaggen, *gnagen, from Old Norse gnaga (“to gnaw”), from Proto-Germanic *gnaganą (“to gnaw”). More at English gnaw.

parole.significato: To gawk; to stare or gape.
parole.testo: A variant of gaum, from Middle English gome, from Old Norse gaumr, from Proto-Germanic *gaumō; compare Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌿𐌼𐌾𐌰𐌽 (gaumjan, “observe”), and see gaum for more. parole.significato: Lacking intelligence, sense or understanding; foolish.
parole.testo: From dialectal English gaum (“heed, attention”) + -less (“without”), from Old Norse gaum, from Proto-Germanic *gaumaz, *gaumō (“heed, attention”). The ‘r’ found in this spelling is a vowel-lengthening device common in non-rhotic dialects of English.

parole.significato: A cuckoo.
parole.testo: From Middle English goke, gowke, from Old Norse gaukr (“cuckoo”), from Proto-Germanic *gaukaz (“cuckoo”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰegʰuǵʰ- (“cuckoo”).

parole.significato: A bowl made of the two hands cupped together.
parole.testo: From Old Norse gaupn (“hollow made by cupped hands”). Doublet of yepsen.

parole.significato: decent, well-meaning, respectable
parole.testo: From earlier graithly, from Middle English graythely, greiþli, greiðlic, from Old Norse greiðligr, equivalent to graith + -ly.

parole.significato: properly, really
parole.testo: From earlier graithly, from Middle English graythely, graydly, graitheli, graithlich, grathliche, graythelyche, from Old Norse greiðliga, equivalent to graith + -ly.

parole.significato: A branch of a tree; a stalk or stem of a plant; an offshoot.
parole.testo: From Middle English grayn, from Old Norse grein (“bough, branch”), from Proto-Germanic *grainiz (“branch, twig, ramification”), of unknown origin. Related to English grove (“thicket”).

parole.significato: To make ready; prepare; put in order; make fit for use.
parole.testo: From Middle English graithen, greithen, graiden, grathen, from Old Norse greiða (“to make ready, prepare, arrange, disentangle”), from Proto-Germanic *garaidijaną (“to prepare, put in order”). parole.significato: Preparation; arrangement; condition.
parole.testo: From Middle English graith, graythe, greithe, from Old Norse greiði (“preparation, arrangement”), from Proto-Germanic *garaidiją (“apparatus, gadget”). parole.significato: A reeve; steward.
parole.testo: From Middle English gryve, grayve, from Old Norse greifi (“a count, earl, steward”), akin to Swedish and Danish greve (“a count, earl”), Old English ġerēfa (“reeve”). More at reeve.

parole.significato: The break (of day); dawn.
parole.testo: Apparently derived from Old Norse grýja (“dawn”); but compare Dutch krieken.

parole.significato: A pig, especially a young pig, or its meat; sometimes specifically, a breed of pig or boar native to north Britain, now…
parole.testo: From Middle English gris, from Old Norse gríss (“male pig; pigling”). Compare Old Dutch gristo, gristio (“boar, wild boar”).

parole.significato: A governor of a town or province.
parole.testo: From Middle English greve, greyve, grave, grafe, from Old Norse greifi, from Middle Low German grēve, grâve, related to Old English grœfa, groefa, variants of Old English ġerēfa (“steward, reeve”). More at reeve.

parole.significato: Guaranteed security, sanctuary, safe conduct.
parole.testo: From Middle English grith, griþ, from Late Old English griþ, from Old Norse grið (“domicile, home”), in the plural with a meaning "truce, peace; sanctuary, asylum". parole.significato: To be prone on the ground.
parole.testo: From Middle English *grovelen, from Old Norse grufla, grœfla (“to grovel”), from Proto-Germanic *grubilōną (“to dig, delve into”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebʰ‑ (“to dig, scrape, scrabble, scratch”); akin to Old Norse á grufu (“on one's belly”) ( > Old Norse grúfa (“to lie face down, grovel”)).

parole.significato: A kind of fiddle or violin played on the Shetland Islands.
parole.testo: Uncertain, perhaps from Old Norse gígja. If so, doublet of gigue.

parole.significato: A recipient of hospitality, especially someone staying by invitation at the house of another.
parole.testo: From Middle English gest, from Old Norse gestr, which replaced or was merged with Old English ġiest, both from Proto-Germanic *gastiz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis (“stranger, guest, host, someone with whom one has reciprocal duties of hospitality”). Doublet of host, from Latin. Cognates West-G

parole.significato: A group or association mainly of tradespeople made up of merchants, craftspeople, or artisans, particularly in the Midd…
parole.testo: From Middle English gilde, from Old Norse gildi (“payment, guild”). Related to geld, yield, yauld.

parole.significato: A device for shooting projectiles or ditto (a shooter), functioning through stored energy: a firearm, cannon, harpoon g…
parole.testo: From Middle English gunne, gonne, possibly from Gunnhild, a female given name formerly used as a nickname for engines of war (compare Nordic Gunn, a female name meaning “battle”). The name is composed of the Norse elements gunnr and hildr, both meaning "battle".

parole.significato: A strong, abrupt rush of wind.
parole.testo: Apparently from an unrecorded Middle English *gust, from Old Norse gustr (“a gust, blast”), from Proto-Germanic *gustiz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰew-. parole.significato: A giantess, typically a giant wife.
parole.testo: From English gyre-carlin, from Old Norse gýgr (“ogress”) + English carline (“old woman”).

parole.significato: A witch.
parole.testo: From Old Norse gýgr (“ogress”) + English carline (“old woman”).

parole.significato: the open sea, especially as a place to fish
parole.testo: From Old Norse haf (“the sea”). Cognate with Danish hav, Old English hæf (Etymology 2).

parole.significato: A small wood, or part of a wood or copse, which is marked off or enclosed for felling, or which has been felled.
parole.testo: From Middle English hag (denoting a gap in a cliff), from Old Norse hǫgg (“cut, gap, breach”), derivative of hǫggva (“to hack, hew”). Compare English hew, Old Swedish hug (“blow, stroke”).

parole.significato: A stackyard, an enclosure on a farm for stacking grain, hay, etc.
parole.testo: From Old Norse heygarðr (“hay-yard”).

parole.significato: A common snake, such as an adder or a viper.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English hagworme (“viper”), from Old Norse hǫggormr (“serpent”), from hǫgg (“stroke, blow”) + ormr (“worm, snake”). Cognate with Icelandic höggormur (“poisonous snake, serpent”), Swedish huggorm (“adder, viper”).

parole.significato: Healthy, whole, safe.
parole.testo: From Middle English heyl (“healthy, sound”), from Old Norse heill, from Proto-Germanic *hailaz (“whole, entire, healthy”). The verb is from Middle English heilen, itself from the adjective. Doublet of whole, hale, and heil.

parole.significato: To hedge or fence in; enclose; protect by hedging.
parole.testo: From earlier hayne, from Middle English *haynen, *heynen, from Old Norse hegna (“to protect; defend”), from Proto-Germanic *haginjaną (“to hedge”), equivalent to hedge + -en. parole.significato: To haul; to hoist.
parole.testo: From Middle English hals (“neck”), from Old Norse háls (“neck, part of the forecastle or bow of a ship”), from Proto-Germanic *halsaz (“neck”). See Etymology 1. Cognate with Danish hals (“neck, tack”).

parole.significato: A female guardian angel in Norse mythology, believed to accompany a person and decide their luck and happiness.
parole.testo: From Old Norse hamingja.

parole.significato: A hold, grasp; custody, power of confining or keeping.
parole.testo: From Middle English hondfast, past participle of Middle English hondfesten (“to betroth”), from Old Norse handfesta (“to strike a bargain, pledge”), itself from hönd (“hand”) + festa (“to fasten, fix, affirm”), perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European root *pHst-.

parole.significato: A lucky omen.
parole.testo: From Middle English handsell, hanselle, from Old English handselen and/or Old Norse handsal (literally “hand-gift”). Cognate with Scots hansel, Danish handsel.

parole.significato: A person's lot (good or bad), luck, fortune, fate.
parole.testo: From Middle English hap, happe (“chance, hap, luck, fortune”), potentially cognate with or from Old English ġehæp (“fit, convenient”) and/or Old Norse happ (“hap, chance, good luck”), from Proto-Germanic *hampą (“convenience, happiness”), from Proto-Indo-European *kob- (“good fortune, prophecy; to b

parole.significato: Unpleasantly rough to the touch or other senses.
parole.testo: From Middle English harsk, harisk(e), hask(e), herris. parole.significato: An object of hatred.
parole.testo: From Middle English haate, hat, hate (noun), probably from Old English hatian (“to hate”, verb) and/or Old Norse hatr (“hate”, noun). parole.significato: A shock of standing sheaves of corn or grain, the tops of which are covered and protected by two sheaves laid in such a…
parole.testo: From Old Norse hǫttr (“cowl or covering”) + -ock (“diminutive suffix”). Compare dialectal Swedish hatt (“the covering of a corn-rick”).

parole.significato: The cereal grain of cultivated oats (Avena sativa).
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English haver, havere, from Old Norse hafri (“oat, oats”), from Proto-Germanic *habrô (“oat, oats”), from Proto-Indo-European *kapro- (“goat”); reinforced by Scots haver in Scotland. Cognate with Dutch haver (“oats”) and German Hafer (“oat”).

parole.significato: Rather.
parole.testo: From Old Norse heldr. Cognate with Danish heller.

parole.significato: To pour.
parole.testo: From Middle English hellen, from Old Norse hella (“to pour”), from Proto-Germanic *halþijaną (“to incline, tip; to pour out, empty”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to lean, incline”). parole.significato: A local leader in early mediaeval Norway.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Norse hersir.

parole.significato: home
parole.testo: From Old Norse heimr, compare Danish hjem. Doublet of home.

parole.significato: To walk with a limp, to drag a limb, to walk lamely; to move with a gait somewhere between walking and crawling.
parole.testo: A word of unknown origin, first recorded in Scots sources from the late fifteenth century; but probably from Old Norse herpast (“to suffer from cramp”) the middle voice verb. Compare the Icelandic herpa (“to contract, to draw together”).

parole.significato: An ancient Norse board game.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Norse hnefatafl (“board game of the fist”), made of hnefi (“fist, the king piece of the hnefatafl game”) and tafl (“a table, a board game”). parole.significato: Used to attract attention to something sighted, usually by lookouts.
parole.testo: From Middle English ho, hoo (interjection), from Old English hō, probably from Old Norse hó! (interjection, also, a shepherd's call). Compare Dutch ho, German ho, Old French ho! (“hold!, halt!”).

parole.significato: A cough.
parole.testo: From Middle English *host, *hoste, from Old Norse hósti (“a cough”), akin to Icelandic hósti, Swedish hosta, Danish hoste (“a cough”). More at whoost.

parole.significato: To cough.
parole.testo: From Middle English *hosten, from Old Norse hósta (“to cough”), from Proto-Germanic *hwōstāną (“to cough”).

parole.significato: A temple, sanctuary, a shrine, or hall.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Norse hof or Old English hof, reinforced in modern (post-1990, chiefly neopagan) use by Icelandic hof (“shrine, temple”).

parole.significato: To behave frivolously and thoughtlessly; to play the fool.
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from Old Norse, or a native Old English term. Perhaps somehow from Middle English hote (“to promise, etc.”). parole.significato: Small island, islet.

parole.significato: In Norse and Icelandic culture, a duel to the death.
parole.testo: From Old Norse hólmganga; cognate with Icelandic hólmganga, Danish holmgang, Swedish holmgång.

parole.significato: Projections located at the masthead or foremast, serving as a support for the trestletrees and top on which to rest; a…
parole.testo: From Middle English hownde, hount, houn, probably from Old Norse húnn, from Proto-Germanic *hūnaz.

parole.significato: A member of the Scandinavian royal household troops.
parole.testo: From Middle English houscarl, from Old English hūscarl, from Old Norse húskarl, equivalent to house + carl. Cognate with Old English hūsċeorl, Old Frisian hūskerl.

parole.significato: An artificial barrow or tumulus; in later folklore, associated with fairies.
parole.testo: From Middle English howe, hough, hogh, partly from Old English hōh (“promontory”), and partly from Old Norse haugr (“a how, mound”). Compare Old French höe (“hillock, hill”), from the same Germanic source.

parole.significato: holly (plant)
parole.testo: From Middle English hulver, hulfere, from Old Norse hulfr (“holly”), akin to English holly.

parole.significato: A platform where candidates in an election give speeches.
parole.testo: From Middle English husting, from Old English hūsting, borrowed from Old Norse húsþing (“house assembly”), from hús (“house”) + þing (“council, meeting”), equivalent to house + thing. Cognate with Icelandic húsþing (“assembly”).

parole.significato: Another name for Logi.
parole.testo: From Old Norse Hálogi (“tall flame”), a compound of hár (“high”) and logi (“fire, blaze”).

parole.significato: Diligent; persistent.

parole.significato: In the middle; between.

parole.significato: Bored or lacking enthusiasm, typically after having been overexposed to, or having consumed too much of something.
parole.testo: From jade (“worn-out horse”), possibly from Old Norse jalda (“mare”). Jade as a term of abuse for a woman dates from 1560.

parole.significato: A medieval Scandinavian nobleman, especially in Norway and Denmark.
parole.testo: From Old Norse jarl, from Proto-Norse ᛖᚱᛁᛚᚨᛉ (erilaʀ). Cognates include Old English eorl. Doublet of earl and eorl.

parole.significato: A member of a race of giants who usually stand in opposition to the Æsir and especially to Thor.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Old Norse jǫtunn, from Proto-Germanic *etunaz (“giant”). Doublet of ettin.

parole.significato: A medieval Scandinavian freeman.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Old Norse karl. Doublet of carl, ceorl, and churl.

parole.significato: a multipurpose intermediate size Viking longship
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Norse karfi, or one of its descendants, potentially Swedish karve, or Danish karve.

parole.significato: A large beam along the underside of a ship’s hull from bow to stern.
parole.testo: From Middle English kele, from Old Norse kjǫlr, itself from Proto-Germanic *keluz, of uncertain origin. Displaced Old English ċēol from a related root. Distantly related to kile.

parole.significato: A round, traditionally wooden container of lesser capacity than a barrel, often used to store beer.
parole.testo: From Middle English kag, from Old Norse kaggi (“keg”), likely a diminutive of Proto-Germanic *kagô (“bush, branch, stalk, stump”). parole.significato: A marshy place or a spring.
parole.testo: From Old Norse kelda (“spring”).

parole.significato: A hook or crook by which a pot is hung over a fire.
parole.testo: From Middle English kelpe, kylpe, from Old Norse kilpr (“the handle of a vessel, loop”). Related to Old Norse kelpa (“otter trap”).

parole.significato: A metaphorical compound or phrase, used especially in Germanic poetry (Old English or Old Norse) whereby a simple thing…
parole.testo: A learned borrowing from Old Norse kenning, from kenna (“to know; to perceive”), from Proto-Germanic *kannijaną (“to make known”); see further at etymology 1. Compare can, keen, ken.

parole.significato: Easily known or seen; obvious; apparent.
parole.testo: Apparently from Old Norse kennispakr (“quick at recognizing persons or things”), from kenna (“know, recognize”) + spakr (“wise”). Compare Swedish kännspak.

parole.significato: An animal belonging to a rare breed of dairy cattle, native to Ireland.
parole.testo: * As an English surname, from a personal name derived from Old Norse Kári. * As an Irish surname, from Ó Ciardha (“descendant of Ciardha”), from ciar (“black”).

parole.significato: Carrion; any filth.
parole.testo: Probably of Old Norse origin like kjǫt (“meat”), from Proto-Germanic *ketwą. Compare Icelandic kjöt (“flesh”); akin to Swedish kött, Danish kød, and Norwegian kjøtt. parole.significato: A strong cleat to which large ropes are belayed.

parole.significato: A bleaching vat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Norse ker (whence also Icelandic ker (“tub”)).

parole.significato: To start (a fire) or light (a torch, a match, coals, etc.).
parole.testo: From Middle English kyndelen, from Old Norse kynda (“to inflame”), from Proto-Germanic *kundijaną.

parole.significato: To snatch; take up hastily; filch
parole.testo: From Middle English kippen, from Old Norse kippa (“to pull; snatch”) or Middle Dutch kippen (“to grasp, seize, catch”). parole.significato: A church.
parole.testo: Inherited from Northern Middle English kirke, borrowed from Old Norse kirkja, borrowed from Old English ċiriċe, from Proto-West Germanic *kirikā, borrowed from Koine Greek κῡρῐᾰκόν (kūrĭăkón), a nominalization of κῡριακός (kūriakós), or from Ancient Greek -ον (-on). parole.significato: A battle-axe or halberd.

parole.significato: A sheaf; a handful (of crops).
parole.testo: From Middle English thrave, threve, thrafe, from Old Norse þrefi (“a bunch or handful of sheaves”), related to Old Norse þrifa (“to grasp”). Cognate with Swedish trave, Danish trave.

parole.significato: The characteristic of using a minimum of something (especially money).
parole.testo: From Middle English thrift, thryfte, þrift, from Old Norse þrift (“thriving condition, prosperity”). Equivalent to thrive + -t.

parole.significato: Eager; earnest; vehement.
parole.testo: From Middle English thro, thra, from Old Norse þrár (“stubborn, obstinate, persevering”), from Proto-Germanic *þrawaz (“obstinate”), from Proto-Indo-European *ter- (“to grind, drill, turn”).

parole.significato: related or pertaining to Trøndelag, Norway, or Thronds
parole.testo: From Thronds + -ish; a calque of Old Norse þrǿnzkr, from þróndr (plural þrǿndir, þrǿndr). Compare Norwegian trøndsk and German dröntisch.

parole.significato: people from Trøndelag
parole.testo: Adapted borrowing of Old Norse þrǿndir, þrǿndr m pl. Compare Old English Þrowendas pl, German Drönter m pl, and Norwegian trønder m or m pl. Doublet of Throwends.

parole.significato: related or pertaining to Throwends or Throwendham
parole.testo: From Throwends + -ish; a calque of Old Norse þrǿnzkr, from þróndr (plural þrǿndir, þrǿndr). Compare Norwegian trøndsk and German dröntisch.

parole.significato: An attack made by moving the sword parallel to its length and landing with the point.
parole.testo: From Middle English þrusten, from Old Norse þrysta, from Proto-Germanic *þrustijaną, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *trewd-.

parole.significato: A kind of ancient poem in Germanic languages, consisting of metrical lists of poetic synonyms for oral recitation.
parole.testo: From Old Norse þula.

parole.significato: big toe
parole.testo: From thumb + toe, perhaps a re-modelling of Middle English thombletō, thummeltō, probably from Old Norse þumaltá (“big-toe”).

parole.significato: A piece of forest land cleared for agriculture or habitation; a clearing.

parole.significato: A hillock.
parole.testo: From Old Norse toft, from Proto-Germanic *tumþiz, from Proto-Indo-European *dem- (“to build”).

parole.significato: Vacant time, leisure.
parole.testo: From Middle English toom, tome, tom, from Old Norse tóm (“vacant time, leisure”), from Proto-Germanic *tōmą (“vacant time, leisure”). Related to Old Norse tómr (“vacant, empty”).

parole.significato: Hard, difficult; wearisome, tedious.
parole.testo: From Middle English tor, tore, toor, from Old Norse tor- (“hard, difficult, wrong, bad”, prefix), from Proto-Germanic *tuz- (“hard, difficult, wrong, bad”), from Proto-Indo-European *dus- (“bad, ill, difficult”). parole.significato: Useless physical things to be discarded; rubbish; refuse.
parole.testo: From Middle English trasch, trassh, probably a dialectal form of *trass (compare Orkney truss, English dialectal trous), from Old Norse tros (“rubbish, fallen leaves and twigs”), perhaps related to Proto-Germanic *þrakjaz (“dirt”). parole.significato: True; trusty; trustworthy; faithful.
parole.testo: From Middle English trig, tryg, from Old Norse tryggr (“loyal, faithful, true”), from Proto-Germanic *triwwiz (“loyal, faithful, true”). Cognate with Old English trīewe (“faithful, loyal, true”). More at true.

parole.significato: a riding (one of three ancient divisions of a county in England)
parole.testo: From Middle English trithing, tridinge, from Old English *þriðing, from Old Norse þriðjungr (“third part”).

parole.significato: A strumpet; a whore.

parole.significato: A tool used in peat cutting, a type of turf spade similar to a cascrom.
parole.testo: From Old Norse torfskeri, from torf (“turf”) + skera (“to cut”), whence also Scottish Gaelic tairsgeir, toirsgeir, treidhsgeir and later forms like toirsgian (assimilated to sgian (“knife”)). Known in print from the early 19th century, but doubtless much older.

parole.significato: The vagina or vulva.
parole.testo: Unknown origin. Possibly cognate with Old Norse þveit (“cut, slit, forest clearing”), and if so a doublet of thwaite. May however simply be onomatopoeic or sound-symbolic.

parole.significato: A mongrel dog.
parole.testo: From Middle English tike, tyke, from Old Norse tík (“female dog”), from Proto-Germanic *tīkō. Compare Icelandic tík, Faroese tík, and Swedish tik, all meaning “bitch, female dog”.

parole.significato: A feeling of fear, horror or disgust.
parole.testo: From Middle English ugge, from Old Norse uggr (“fear, apprehension, dread”), related to Old Norse ógn (“terror, threat, dispute”) and agi (“terror, strife, fear, punishment”). More at awe.

parole.significato: To dread, loathe or disgust.
parole.testo: From Middle English uggen, from Old Norse ugga (“to fear”), see above.

parole.significato: Displeasing to the eye; aesthetically unpleasing.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English ugly, uggely, uglike, borrowed from Old Norse uggligr (“fearful, dreadful, horrible in appearance”), from uggr (“fear, apprehension, dread”) (possibly related to agg (“strife, hate”)), equivalent to ug + -ly. parole.significato: Inconsistent with established standards of good form or taste.
parole.testo: From Middle English unsemli, probably a partial calque of Old Norse úsǽmiligr (“unseemly”); equivalent to un- + seemly. Cognate with Icelandic ósæmileg (“offensive”), Norwegian usømmelig (“unseemly”), Danish usømmelig (“unseemly”), German unziemlich.

parole.significato: Faithless; distrustful.
parole.testo: From Middle English untrust, untriste, probably from Old Norse útraustr (“untrustworthy”). Cognate with Icelandic útraustur.

parole.significato: One of the three Norns; the Norn of those who were.
parole.testo: From Old Norse Urðr, from Proto-Germanic *wurdiz (“fate, destiny”), Proto-Indo-European *wert- (“to turn, wind”). Cognate with English weird.

parole.significato: A symbol consisting of three interlocked triangles, used by ancient Germanic peoples, but of uncertain meaning.
parole.testo: Derived from Old Norse valr (“the slain”) and Old Norse knútr (“a knot”), meaning "knot of the slain". The term was coined in later history, as it is not known what name was used by the historical Norse.

parole.significato: Any of the female attendants of Odin, figures said to guide fallen warriors from the battlefield to Valhalla.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Norse valkyrja sg (“chooser of the slain”), plural valkyrjur pl, from Proto-Germanic *walakuzjǭ. Cognate to Old English wælcyrġe. First attested in English as a proper noun (Valkyries) in the 1770s; attested as a common noun (valkyries) since the 1880s.

parole.significato: To take; undertake for.

parole.significato: A Norn song or rhyme, a ballad in Shetland or Orkney.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Old Norse vísa (“verse, strophe, stanza”) (perhaps via Norn [Term?]), whence also Danish vise (“song, ballad, ditty”).

parole.significato: A sorcerer in Norse Heathen societies.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Norse vitki.

parole.testo: From Old Norse vǫlva (völva in modern Icelandic).

parole.significato: An amorphous, compact mass.

parole.testo: From Old Norse val (“choice”). Compare Icelandic velja (“to choose”). More at wale.

parole.testo: From Middle English weyven (“to wave, waver”), from Old Norse veifa (“to wave, swing”) (Norwegian veiva), from Proto-Germanic *waibijaną.

parole.significato: Something selected as being the best, preference; choice; choosing.

parole.significato: Spring, springtime.
parole.testo: From Middle English ware, from Old Norse vár (“spring”), from Proto-Germanic *wazrą. Cognate with Icelandic vor (“spring”), Swedish vår (“spring”), Danish vår (“spring”), Scots ware, wair (“spring”).

parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Old Norse vargr (“wolf”), reintroduced by J. R. R. Tolkien; compare also Old English wearg. The verb senses emerged from the use of warg in George R. R. Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire novels as a noun referring to a person with a magical skin-changing ability.

parole.significato: A toast to health, usually on a festive occasion.
parole.testo: From Middle English wassail, from Old Norse ves heill (“be healthy!”), from the imperative of vesa (“to be”) + heill (“healthy”). parole.significato: A ford.
parole.testo: From Middle English wath, from Old Norse vað (“a ford”). Cognate with Scots wath, Swedish vad. Related to wade.

parole.testo: From Middle English weven (“to wander”); probably from Old Norse veifa (“move around, wave”), related to Latin vibrare.

parole.testo: From Middle English weylawey, from Old English weġ lā weġ, alteration of wā lā wā, with substitution of Old Norse vei for Old English wā. Compare wellawo, weila.

parole.significato: A person from the west.
parole.testo: From west + man. A calque of Old Norse vestmaðr, from vest (“west”) + maðr (“man”).

parole.significato: To breathe hard, and with an audible piping or whistling sound, as persons affected with asthma.
parole.testo: From Middle English whesen, perhaps from Old Norse hvæsa (“to hiss”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwes- (“to pant”).

parole.significato: To move or vibrate (something) with a buzzing sound.
parole.testo: From Middle English whirren, probably from Old Norse: compare Danish hvirre, virre, Norwegian kvirre, Old Norse hvirfla (“to whirl, spread”).

parole.significato: A quick, light sweeping motion.
parole.testo: From Middle English whisk, borrowed from Old Norse visk, from Proto-Germanic *wiskaz, *wiskō (“bundle of hay, wisp”), from Proto-Indo-European *weys-. parole.significato: Stop (especially when commanding a horse or imitative thereof); calm down; slow down.

parole.significato: The state of being a whore, prostitution; sexual indulgence, fornication.
parole.testo: From Middle English horedom, hordom, from Old Norse hórdómr, ultimately corresponding to whore + -dom. Cognate with Swedish hordom (“whoredom”), Middle Dutch hoerdom (“whoredom”).

parole.significato: Brave, valorous, strong.

parole.significato: Wandering; devious.
parole.testo: From Middle English wilsum, wilsom, wildsom, probably after Old Norse villusamr (“erroneous, false”), equivalent to will (“wild”) + -some. Cognate with Scots wilsum (“treacherous, wandering”).

parole.significato: A windlass.

parole.significato: A second or reciprocal distress of other goods in lieu of goods which were taken by a first distress and have been eloi…

parole.significato: Knowledge, awareness.
